vision: Launchway is one place to host your code, build it, test it, scan it and deliver it, on servers you control or as a hosted service.

It aims to be complete without being complicated: every task is a guided wizard, every capability is also in the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and Terraform, and the only things it needs are a database and Git.
AI helps where you ask for it and stays off where you do not, and every run, change and approval is a durable record you can audit.

available.title: Pipelines as code
available.value: Typed YAML with steps, dependencies, run inputs, outputs passed between steps and loops, kept in Git next to the code they build.

available.title: Flow control
available.value: Conditions on steps, retries with back-off, lanes that make runs take turns, run timeouts, and re-running from any step with what each step was given.

available.title: Build caches
available.value: Dependencies kept between runs in the database, with entries a pull request can write but the default branch never reads.

available.title: Triggers
available.value: Push, pull request (with target-branch filters, and newer pushes cancelling older runs), manual, schedule and webhook.

available.title: Shared libraries
available.value: Templates and scripts in their own repository, pinned by tag, branch or commit, with typed parameters.

available.title: Step resources
available.value: Each step is sized, with defaults per kind of step and a ceiling no step can pass, so one step cannot starve a cluster.

available.title: Configuration in the database
available.value: Projects, runner pools, environments, policies, models and more are objects in the database with history, audit and safe concurrent edits, never a file to hand-edit.

available.title: Four levels
available.value: Installation, organisation, unit and project, with names you choose and levels nobody uses kept out of sight.

available.title: Guided setup wizards
available.value: First-run setup, connecting a repository, adding a runner, an environment, a policy or a verification step: plain questions, explained options, answers checked as you go.

available.title: A guided interface
available.value: A Home page that says what to do next with a setup checklist, navigation whose sections and tabs appear only when there is something to show, and a run page that says why each wait is happening.

available.title: One capability, every interface
available.value: What the web UI does, the HTTP API, the command line and the agent endpoint do too, with a table in the build that fails when one falls behind.

available.title: High availability
available.value: Several servers on one PostgreSQL database with no leader; a run survives a server or a runner dying. SQLite for a single server.

available.title: Quality gates
available.value: Lint, size, architecture, test and originality checks fail the build, so the code stays easy to change.

available.title: GitOps with Argo CD
available.value: Deploy by Git commit, watch sync and health, control Argo Rollouts (promote, abort, retry), roll back, lock environments.

available.title: Applications view
available.value: The Argo CD applications a deploy runner has seen, shown with their status next to your environments.

available.title: Verification after a deploy
available.value: Checks on Prometheus, Loki, ClickHouse and OpenSearch with automatic abort or rollback; an optional model explains the verdict and never turns a failure into a pass.

available.title: Container images
available.value: Rootless builds, scans, signatures, provenance and SBOMs, pushed to any OCI registry.

available.title: Approvals and protected environments
available.value: Approval steps; the person who started a run cannot approve its production deploy.

available.title: Policy gates
available.value: Rules pipelines cannot opt out of, at run start, before deploys and image pushes; report or enforce; audited, expiring waivers.

available.title: Sign-in and access
available.value: OpenID Connect sign-in with groups, roles per project and environment, scoped API tokens and an audit trail.

available.title: Secrets that stay with runners
available.value: Pipelines hold references; runners read values from Vault, OpenBao, files or the environment, and mask them.

available.title: Security findings and SBOMs
available.value: Secret, code, dependency, licence and image findings (SARIF), new and fixed across runs, and a component search.

available.title: Secure step execution
available.value: Non-root step pods under strict pod security, a step pod removed when its run ends and leaked ones reaped, container and host executors, and runners that only connect outward.

available.title: Runner identity and pools
available.value: Join tokens, a key per runner, pools scoped to projects, and allow-lists on the runner itself.

available.title: Test, coverage and HTML reports
available.value: Thirteen test formats, coverage with thresholds, flaky-test detection, history, and the tools' own HTML reports in a sandbox.

available.title: Built-in artifact storage
available.value: Artifacts and hosted reports live in the database by default, so several servers need nothing else; S3 or a shared folder are optional.

available.title: AI models in steps
available.value: Optional hosted or local models for steps and failure explanations, with per-model token limits; keys never enter a step's container.

available.title: An endpoint for agents
available.value: Agents validate pipelines, start and watch runs and diagnose failures with exactly the rights of the token they hold.

available.title: Open source
available.value: Free software under the AGPL-3.0, with a commercial licence for those who cannot use it, and this documentation site with its roadmap.

available.title: A public documentation site and roadmap
available.value: Enterprise-level documentation with diagrams, security guidance, a graphical roadmap with drill-down pages, and a local demo.

milestones.name: Host your code and run your pipelines in one place
milestones.promise: A team can keep its repositories in Launchway, review and merge there, and run every pipeline it has, with everything a hosted CI service offers and nothing else to install.
milestones.audience: Teams that want one product for their code and their builds, and teams that keep their code on another host but want Launchway to run the pipelines and report back.
milestones.what: Milestone 1 makes Launchway a complete home for day-to-day engineering. Code can live in Launchway or stay where it is; either way people review changes, see every check on the change, and run every pipeline they had on a hosted CI service. The interface follows a change from idea to running software so a beginner can find their way.
scenarios: You push a branch and open a change. The page shows the pipeline running, the tests and findings as they arrive, and a plain sentence saying what stops it from merging.
A teammate suggests a one-line fix in review and you apply it with one click; the checks run again by themselves.
You keep your code on another host. Launchway runs the pipeline and writes the result back to the pull request, and a failing run blocks the merge there too.
You re-run a failed run from the third step, and the first two steps use what they produced last time.
A new colleague opens Home and is told, in order, what to set up next.

milestones.diagramNote: A change from push to merge. The built-in host and a connected host look the same to the pipeline engine.
done: A repository can be created, cloned, pushed to, reviewed and merged in Launchway, and a deliberate failure of a server during a push never loses an acknowledged push.
A written acceptance suite for hosting passes, including importing from another host.
A pull request on a connected host receives a status from Launchway and cannot be merged when the run fails.
Every pipeline feature in the milestone has a reference page and a worked example.
Every setting introduced has a command, an API call, an agent tool and a Terraform resource, checked by a test.
A new user can complete setup from Home without editing a file.
notIncluded: Custom step languages, generated pipelines and the visual designer (Milestone 2).

groups.name: Host your code
groups.blurb: Launchway stores your repositories and serves them, so one product and a database are enough.

items.title: Built-in Git hosting
items.value: Launchway stores your repositories and serves them over HTTPS and SSH, with storage designed so that no acknowledged push is ever lost.
items.detail: A push, over HTTPS or SSH, is acknowledged only once it is durable, and any server in a group can serve any repository because servers keep nothing that matters on their own disks. This is the base every other hosting item stands on.
items.needs: A database; the shared blob store that already exists.

items.title: Safe storage and failover for repositories
items.value: If a server or the database fails over, every acknowledged push is still there.
items.detail: Refs and their history live in the database with an atomic update, content lives in the blob store, and servers hold only disposable caches. A test kills servers mid-push and the pass mark is that nothing acknowledged is lost.

items.title: Git over SSH
items.value: Clone, fetch and push over SSH with your own keys, beside HTTPS.
items.detail: User keys and per-repository read-only deploy keys are listed and revocable in one place, the server proves itself with a protected host key that stays the same across servers, and SSH uses the same permissions, limits and audit as HTTPS. Run-scoped read-only credentials mean a pipeline holds a credential only while it runs.

items.title: Create, rename, archive and set visibility
items.value: The everyday repository lifecycle: create, rename with redirects, transfer, archive as read-only, and private, internal or public visibility.
items.detail: The same wizard connects an existing repository from another host or creates a hosted one, so people do not need to learn two flows. Old addresses keep working after a rename.

items.title: Browse and search your code
items.value: History, file history, blame, raw files, archives, permanent links with line ranges, and a go-to-file finder.
items.detail: Reading code is where most of the time goes, so it has to be quick and linkable. The newest commit is drawn on its journey above the file tree, so you see where the change is, not only what it contains.

items.title: Search inside a repository
items.value: Find text and file names in the branch you are looking at.
items.detail: Search runs on a disposable cache with bounded resources, so there is no index to keep in step. Results also cover pipeline files, templates and steps.

items.title: Show every kind of file properly
items.value: Markdown, diagrams, math, tables of data, images with before and after, documents and notebooks render in the browser.
items.detail: Pipeline files also render as a drawing beside the text. Rendering is sandboxed so a file can never run anything.

items.title: Edit in the browser, as a commit
items.value: Edit, upload, delete and create a branch from the web page; every save is a real commit.
items.detail: This is the same commit path the pipeline editor uses, so there is one way a change gets into Git. Cherry-pick, revert and patch download are there too.

items.title: Verified commits and tags
items.value: Verify signatures on commits and tags, manage signing keys, and let a rule require signed commits.
items.detail: A verified state is a fact a branch rule or a deployment policy can ask for, so an unsigned change cannot reach production if you say so.

items.title: Repository maintenance and health
items.value: Scheduled housekeeping, an integrity check, a size report and a health note on the home page.
items.detail: Problems appear in the same attention list as everything else instead of being found when a push is slow. Maintenance runs as separate programs, not inside the server.

items.title: Repository trash
items.value: A deleted repository goes to a trash and can come back within a set time.
items.detail: Delete is reversible for a period you choose, and both the delete and the restore are in the audit trail.

items.title: Mirrors in and out
items.value: Pull a repository from another host on a schedule, or push every change to another host as a safety copy.
items.detail: Status, last error and lag show on the home page and raise an alert, so a stale mirror is noticed. A pull mirror lets teams move over at their own pace.

items.title: Repository settings screens
items.value: Collaborators, access, tokens, webhooks, merge options and feature switches, each as a plain screen.
items.detail: Features that are switched off are hidden, so a small project stays small. Each screen explains what it does in a sentence.

items.title: Branch and tag manager
items.value: List, rename, delete and restore branches, set the default, and delete merged branches automatically.
items.detail: It also shows the last pipeline result on every branch, so stale or broken branches are easy to spot.

items.title: Large files
items.value: Store large binary files outside the normal history, with locks and quotas.
items.detail: Quotas and usage are shown next to the repository. The runner image includes the tooling, so builds fetch large files without extra setup.

items.title: Forks and templates
items.value: Fork a repository to propose changes from your own copy, and start new repositories from templates.
items.detail: A template can carry a pipeline and an environment setup, so a new repository arrives with a working path to production. Fork runs follow the rule that untrusted code never sees secrets.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Repository quotas and size limits
items.value: Limits on repository size, large-file storage and per-organisation usage, shared with artifact and log quotas.
items.detail: One quota model for everything that takes space, with warnings before a limit is reached.

items.title: Activity, language and topic information
items.value: Contributor activity, commit graphs, languages, topics and a repository picture.
items.detail: Delivery information such as deployment frequency and lead time sits on the same page, because Launchway already knows it.

items.title: Webhooks to other tools
items.value: Send repository events to chat tools and any web address, with a delivery log, retries and test deliveries.
items.detail: One notification channel set is shared with pipelines and approvals. Payloads are signed, and compatible shapes are offered so existing tools keep working.

items.title: Notifications and email
items.value: An inbox, watching and muting, and email for mentions, reviews and failures, including replying by email.
items.detail: Sending mail is optional and off until configured. The same preferences cover review, work item and pipeline events.

groups.name: Review and merge changes
groups.blurb: Pull requests that show the run, the tests and the policy verdict on one page.

items.title: Pull requests on the built-in host
items.value: Open, review, discuss and merge changes inside Launchway, with branch rules that block a merge until required checks pass.
items.detail: A pull request page shows its pipeline run, tests, coverage change, findings, policy verdict, preview environment and deployment together, with no round trip through a webhook. Expected results are written in the same step that accepts the push, so a change never looks mergeable before its checks exist.

items.title: Review with inline comments and suggestions
items.value: Comment on lines and ranges, suggest a change the author can apply in one click, and mark files as viewed.
items.detail: Comments stay attached to the right lines when new revisions are pushed. Reviewers choose approve, request changes or comment, and the verdict belongs to a revision.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Branch rules and protected tags
items.value: Required approvals, stale-approval dismissal, blocked merges, linear history, protected branches and tags that cannot move.
items.detail: The page says in plain words why a change cannot land yet and what would unblock it. A tag pinned by a template resolves to a commit and is recorded on the run.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Code owners
items.value: Name who must review changes to which paths, using people or groups.
items.detail: Owners can be the group that owns the deployment environment, so the people who run a service review the changes to it.
items.needs: Review with inline comments and suggestions.

items.title: Merge styles and auto-merge
items.value: Merge, squash, rebase and fast-forward, and merge automatically when the checks pass.
items.detail: Auto-merge is driven by events, not polling. A manually merged marker handles changes landed outside Launchway.

items.title: Merge queue
items.value: Queue approved changes and test the real merged result with the real pipeline before it lands.
items.detail: The queue is visible on each change, so people see where they stand and why a change was held back.

items.title: Resolve conflicts in the browser
items.value: See the conflict, choose a side or edit, and finish the merge on the page.
items.detail: Conflict detection runs as soon as the target moves, so the page tells you early.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Findings and failures on the diff
items.value: Security findings and test failures appear as notes on the lines they concern.
items.detail: The same results feed the policy verdict, so what you read on the line is what blocks the merge.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Templates for changes and work
items.value: Templates that pre-fill the description of a pull request or work item, and issue forms.
items.detail: Teams keep their expectations in one place and new contributors get a prompt instead of a blank box.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Pull-request status everywhere
items.value: Report each run back to the pull request as a status and block a merge that does not pass, on the built-in host and on every connected one.
items.detail: A connected host that has no status feature gets the same result as a comment and an approval, so the rule is the same everywhere.

groups.name: Work items and decisions
groups.blurb: Track work, decisions and releases next to the code.

items.title: Issues and work items
items.value: Track work next to the code, with labels, milestones, assignees and links between items, and link every change to the reason for it.
items.detail: An item also traces to commits, runs and deployments, so the question which environment a request reached has a one-click answer.

items.title: Labels, milestones and templates for work
items.value: Coloured and exclusive labels, milestones with progress, and templates and forms for new items.
items.detail: Labels and milestones are shared across projects at the levels you choose.

items.title: Dependencies and parent items
items.value: Mark that one item blocks another, and group items under a parent.
items.detail: A blocked item drops out of the list of what is ready next, for people and for agents.

items.title: Boards that show delivery
items.value: A board with custom columns whose cards show where the change is: in review, building, in a test environment, in production.
items.detail: The board is the same data as the list, drawn differently.

items.title: Decision records
items.value: A question, the options, a recommendation, what it blocks, and the answer with who gave it and when.
items.detail: Decisions are reviewed and answered in bulk in the interface. They are first-class records, so months later you can find why something was done.

items.title: Import and sync from other trackers
items.value: Bring issues in from other trackers, or keep them in sync in both directions while you switch.
items.detail: Six trackers are supported equally. A dry run reports counts before anything is written.

items.title: Optional time tracking and due dates
items.value: Estimates, timers and due dates, off until a project turns them on.
items.detail: Time joins the delivery chain, so effort can be read next to lead time.

items.title: Confidential items and links to the code
items.value: Items visible only to chosen people, and branches started from an item that carry its reference.
items.detail: Confidentiality uses the same permission model as everything else, so nothing leaks across a boundary. The branch name needs no typing to stay traceable.

items.title: A wiki per repository
items.value: A wiki that is itself a Git repository, with history, linked live to pipelines and deployments.
items.detail: Pages can show current status. A vault of notes can stay in step with it (see the Obsidian sync).

items.title: Static pages
items.value: Publish a static site from a branch of a repository, built by a pipeline.
items.detail: The site is served by Launchway with its own address and the same access rules as the repository.

items.title: Releases with notes and evidence
items.value: Releases with tags, notes, attachments and drafts, with notes grouped by work item and marked with where each change reached.
items.detail: A release is a signed record of what was actually deployed, with its images, provenance and approvals attached automatically.

groups.name: People and access on the host
groups.blurb: Accounts, organisations, tokens and administration for the built-in host.

items.title: Organisations, teams and collaborators
items.value: Teams with their own permissions on repositories, and invitations for people from outside.
items.detail: One permission model covers code, work items, pipelines and environments, so there is no second set of users to maintain.

items.title: Tokens and scoped access
items.value: Personal and service tokens limited to chosen repositories and actions.
items.detail: Tokens use the same audit trail and limits as sign-in sessions. Service accounts are for tools, not people.

items.title: Launchway as a sign-in provider
items.value: Let other tools sign in with accounts that live in Launchway.
items.detail: Useful for small teams that run a handful of internal tools and want one place for identity.

items.title: Host administration screens
items.value: Users, repositories, queues, background tasks, a banner and a maintenance mode.
items.detail: Everything an administrator checks daily is on one set of pages, and it is also available through the API and the command line.

items.title: Compatible addresses and tools
items.value: Clone addresses, push events and read interfaces shaped like the common ones, so existing remotes, bots and editors keep working.
items.detail: This makes moving over a matter of changing a setting, not rewriting scripts.

items.title: Languages and themes
items.value: A translated interface, light and dark, and custom themes.
items.detail: Accessibility checks are part of the build, so a theme cannot ship with unreadable text.

groups.name: Move your repositories in
groups.blurb: A tested path from another Git host, so switching is a step and not a leap.

items.title: Move your repositories in
items.value: Import repositories, issues, pull requests, labels, milestones, releases and wikis from another Git host, and keep a mirror back while you switch.
items.detail: Counts are reported one for one and a dry run shows what would happen first. Moving can be done a team at a time.

items.title: An acceptance suite for hosting
items.value: A written end-to-end suite that hosting must pass before it is called ready, so that switching is a tested step, not a leap.
items.detail: Each requirement a team has of its current host becomes a check, run against Launchway before and after the switch. It is also the proof anyone can read.

items.title: A complete Git forge
items.value: Discussions, snippets, notifications, activity feeds and the rest of a hosted Git service, in order of value, with an interface that is better integrated than a stand-alone one.
items.detail: Everything here is optional and off until chosen. The point is that people who want a single place do not have to give up the usual features.

items.title: Replacing a self-hosted Git server
items.value: A guide and a checklist for retiring a self-hosted Git server in favour of Launchway.
items.detail: Covers moving, redirects, users, hooks, integrations, backups and a rollback plan, with each step verified by the acceptance suite.

groups.name: Keep your Git host, if you prefer
groups.blurb: Launchway works with the host you already use. Hosting is optional.

items.title: Every Git host, equally
items.value: First-class connections to every major Git host, including GitHub, AWS CodeCommit and self-managed ones, with each one's limits stated plainly in the docs and the wizards.
items.detail: Each host passes the same conformance suite as the built-in one. A host that has not yet passed is labelled so until it does.

items.title: Self-managed variants of hosts
items.value: Hosts you run yourself, with their own addresses and certificates, are first-class.
items.detail: Setup asks for the address and trust, nothing more. Each variant's differences are stated in the wizard.

items.title: Hosts without webhooks
items.value: Hosts that cannot call Launchway are watched through polling or a bridge from their event service.
items.detail: The result is the same: a push starts a run. Launchway posts status as a comment and an approval where the host has no status feature.

items.title: One identity across hosts
items.value: Map the same person on different hosts to one Launchway user.
items.detail: Reviews, approvals and audit entries are then attributed to a person, not to a host account.

items.title: A common provider model
items.value: One internal contract every host, including the built-in one, must satisfy.
items.detail: The built-in host is a provider like the others, so a feature that works on one works on all, or the docs say it does not.

groups.name: Pipelines that match what teams expect from hosted CI
groups.blurb: Everything a hosted CI service offers, in one place.

items.title: Conditions, retries, lanes and re-runs
items.value: Run a step only when it should, retry what is flaky, make runs take turns, and re-run from any step.
items.detail: Re-running from a step keeps what each earlier step was given, so a fix does not mean starting over.

items.title: Warm builds with caches
items.value: Keep dependencies between runs so builds start warm, with rules for who may read and write them.
items.detail: A pull request can write an entry the default branch never reads, which removes the cache-poisoning risk.

items.title: Flow control, part two
items.value: Services with readiness checks and logs, a runner and workspace of their own per step, approval quorums, and loops that tolerate chosen members.
items.detail: This completes the control a complex pipeline needs without dropping into scripts.

items.title: Platform matrices
items.value: Run the same steps across operating systems and architectures from one definition.
items.detail: Results show as one grid with a failure marked where it happened. Runners with the right platform are chosen automatically.

items.title: Cloud sign-in per step
items.value: Each step proves its identity to a cloud with short-lived tokens, so no long-lived cloud keys are stored.
items.detail: The trust is set up in the cloud once, and the token carries the project, branch and environment.

items.title: Re-run only what failed
items.value: Re-run just the failed steps of a run, with earlier results reused. Re-running from a chosen step already works.
items.detail: Combined with caches, a flaky test costs minutes instead of a full run.

items.title: Per-step runner and workspace
items.value: Each step can choose its own image, runner and working area.
items.detail: A step that needs a large machine or special hardware asks for it without moving the whole pipeline.

groups.name: A guided interface a complete beginner can use
groups.blurb: Everything by clicking, with every page saying what it is for and what to do next.

items.title: Follow a change on its launch line
items.value: A single line that shows one change travelling from idea to running software, with each station opening its evidence.
items.detail: Choose a station and its review, tests, image, place or decision opens underneath. This is the page that answers where is my change and is it all right.

items.title: A Home that tells you what to do next
items.value: One sentence about what needs you, rows with one recommended action each, and a checklist that disappears as you finish it.
items.detail: When nothing needs anyone it becomes a calm all-clear page with the board of changes in flight.

items.title: Six plainly named sections
items.value: A short, plainly named set of sections, with the ones that have nothing to show kept out of sight, replaces a long flat menu.
items.detail: Anything switched off is not shown, so a new installation is small and grows as you turn things on.

items.title: Overview, then focus, then detail
items.value: Every topic follows one pattern: a picture of what is going on, one thing in focus, then everything about it for engineers.
items.detail: Pages link to each other in context, so you follow a problem instead of searching a menu.

items.title: Nothing lost for a nicer look
items.value: Every detail the current interface shows is kept, and the new one adds to it.
items.detail: Each screen of today has a recorded place in the new layout, and a check confirms nothing has been dropped.

items.title: A do bar for every task
items.value: A search box that finds pages and starts guided actions such as turn a toggle off or why did this fail.
items.detail: It reaches everything without adding to the menu.

items.title: Decision cards that read on a phone
items.value: An approval is a card with what, who, risk, evidence and what happens next, readable in seconds.
items.detail: Reject needs a reason. A decision can be undone until it has acted.

items.title: Pipelines drawn as living lines
items.value: A pipeline appears as stations on tracks, with parallel steps splitting and joining, live while it runs.
items.detail: Selecting a station shows its facts, and the log sits under the line.

items.title: Light, dark and phone widths
items.value: The same interface in light and dark and on a phone, with an accessibility check as a build gate.
items.detail: Charts say where they came from and never rely on colour alone.

groups.name: Move your existing pipelines over
groups.blurb: Bring pipelines across in waves, without surprises.

items.title: A converter and a move-over guide
items.value: Bring pipelines written for other CI services across in waves, with a report of anything that needs a person.
items.detail: The converter says what it could not translate, and why. The guide covers running both side by side while you compare results.

items.title: Run old and new side by side
items.value: Compare a Launchway run with the run it replaces and see where results differ.
items.detail: This is how a team gains confidence before switching.
items.needs: A converter and a move-over guide.

groups.name: Foundations that finish alongside
groups.blurb: The groundwork that every other item stands on.

items.title: Terraform provider
items.value: Every kind of setting managed as code, each new kind shipping with its resource, so nothing is reachable only by clicking.
items.detail: A test fails the build when an object exists without its Terraform resource. The provider ships beside the server.

items.title: Database failover and no lost push
items.value: High availability that covers the database and repository storage as well as the servers.
items.detail: Failover is rehearsed in tests with writes in flight.

items.title: Launchway builds and deploys itself
items.value: Launchway is built, tested, signed and rolled out by Launchway, in a group of servers, with rollouts and checks.
items.detail: Runners on virtual machines and customer machines update themselves too (see the runner update item). The pipeline and the runbook are written and checked; a first real run, with its rollback, is still to come.

items.title: Fewer concepts to learn
items.value: No pile of connectors, services and environments to define before anything works.
items.detail: Six words cover everyday use: project, pipeline, step, run, environment and runner.

items.title: Signed releases and installers
items.value: Reproducible release builds with SBOMs, deb and rpm packages, an install script for runners and a runner-only Helm chart, with signing and provenance in the release workflow.
items.detail: All of it has been exercised on a machine of its own. The release workflow has not yet run for real, so no release is published; until then, build from source.

milestones.name: Deeper pipeline power, and a way off self-hosted automation servers
milestones.promise: Pipelines can be as dynamic as real code needs, and a team running an automation server can move its jobs without losing what it relies on.
milestones.audience: Teams whose pipelines need real code, many repositories sharing logic, or a move away from a self-hosted automation server.
milestones.what: Milestone 2 makes pipelines as dynamic as real code needs without giving up checking. Steps become programs you test, pipelines can be generated, conditions are typed, and you can design visually. Teams on automation servers get a tested gap analysis and an importer.
scenarios: You write a deployment step in the language your team already uses, test it on your laptop, and share it as a pinned version.
A step looks at the repository and prints the extra steps it needs; Launchway checks them and shows them on the run.
You drag a step onto a pipeline and see the exact lines it will change in Git before you save.
A message on a queue starts a pipeline, and a rejected message is visible with the reason.
You import jobs from an automation server and read a report of what needs a person.
milestones.diagram:
flowchart TD Repo["Repository
pipeline file, step programs"] --> Plan["Check and expand
schema, types, policy"] Gen["Generated steps"] --> Plan Trig["Triggers
push, queue, schedule"] --> Plan Plan --> Graph["Run graph"] Graph --> Steps["Steps in sandboxes"] Steps -->|typed outputs| Graph Designer["Visual designer"] <-->|same file| Repo Catalogue["Catalogue of templates and steps"] --> Repo
milestones.diagramNote: Text, designer and generated steps all end in one checked definition.
done: A custom step in at least three languages runs from a published contract and is unit-tested outside Launchway.
A generated pipeline is checked against the same schema and policy as a written one.
Expressions are checked before a run and have no loops or side effects.
The designer and the text editor produce identical files for identical pipelines.
The gap analysis lists every gap with a test, and each gap is closed or recorded as a decision.
Runners on virtual machines update under policy without manual work.

groups.name: Write pipelines your way
groups.blurb: Pipelines as real programs, checked before they run.

items.title: Custom steps in your own language
items.value: A step is a program in your repository with typed inputs, outputs and secrets, runnable and testable on its own, so pipeline logic is ordinary tested code.
items.detail: You write the step in a language you already use and unit-test it like any application. A template is the interface and the code is what runs.

items.title: A step contract and starter kits
items.value: A published contract for what a step receives and returns, with starter kits for common languages.
items.detail: Starter kits include the types, a local test harness and an example, so the first step takes minutes.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Steps run in a sandbox
items.value: Custom steps run in an isolated container with only the secrets and network they declared.
items.detail: A shared step cannot read what it was not given, which makes sharing steps across teams safe.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Share and pin steps and templates
items.value: Publish a custom step, not only a template, from a repository and pin users to a tag, branch or commit. Pinning templates this way already works.
items.detail: Releases are plain Git tags, so versions, history and review use the tools you already have.

items.title: Generated pipelines
items.value: A step can print more steps in any language; Launchway checks them against the same schema and policy and shows them on the run.
items.detail: This gives the freedom of a script with the safety of a checked definition, and it makes dynamic pipelines possible without file-first configuration.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Expressions for conditions
items.value: A small typed expression language with no loops and no side effects, checked before the run; today's conditions keep working.
items.detail: Because expressions cannot loop or change anything, a pipeline is always checkable without running it.

items.title: Typed outputs between steps
items.value: A step declares what it passes on, and a reference to an output that does not exist fails before the run, not in the middle of it.
items.detail: Types make the earlier values on a re-run knowable, which keeps restarting from a step honest.

items.title: A browsable catalogue of templates and steps
items.value: Shared libraries pinned by tag already work; the catalogue lets you find, compare and update them from inside the product.
items.detail: Each entry shows who uses it, what it needs and which version is current, with an update shown as a change you can review.

items.title: Update notices for shared libraries
items.value: See which projects use an old version of a template and open an update as a reviewable change.
items.detail: Teams keep common pipeline logic current without a manual hunt.
items.needs: A browsable catalogue of templates and steps.

items.title: A triggers page
items.value: One page showing every trigger and exactly which pipelines it starts.
items.detail: You can answer what starts this pipeline and what does this trigger start without opening files.

items.title: Event sources from queues and buses
items.value: Start pipelines from message queues and event buses, with filters, and replies back.
items.detail: Filters, retries and a dead-letter view show what arrived and what was ignored.

items.title: Steps as a graph of containers
items.value: Lay steps out as a graph of containers with fan-out and join, for work that is not a straight line.
items.detail: Each node shows its own logs and result, and the graph is the same object whether drawn or written.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Runners that keep themselves updated
items.value: Runners on VMs and on customers' machines update under your policy, so the fleet never drifts.
items.detail: Hosted pools update automatically, self-hosted pools are notified, and Kubernetes runners follow the chart.

items.title: Pipeline history and flaky tests
items.value: Duration charts, pass rate and the slowest steps across runs, and flaky tests flagged on the pull request. Flaky detection and test history already work on the run page.
items.detail: Flaky tests are marked on the run and on the pull request, so they are quarantined instead of argued over.

items.title: Step pages
items.value: Each step has a page: where its code lives, its inputs and types, and which pipelines use it.
items.detail: Before changing a step, you see who it would affect.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

groups.name: Design visually
groups.blurb: Draw it, read it as text, and see that both are the same thing.

items.title: A visual pipeline designer
items.value: Drag built-in and custom steps into place; it edits the same pipeline file as the text editor, so the two are views of one thing.
items.detail: The designer shows the lines it will change in Git before you save, and saving is a reviewable change. Nothing is stored outside the file.

items.title: A drawing canvas and diagrams
items.value: Architecture diagrams drawn in Launchway beside generated ones and Mermaid.
items.detail: Diagrams are saved as files in Git and exported safely, so documentation and architecture drawings live beside the code.

items.title: Generated architecture views
items.value: Views of your delivery and runtime drawn from what Launchway knows, always current.
items.detail: Applications, pipelines and environments appear as diagrams you can paste into a document.

items.title: Two-way Obsidian sync
items.value: Export and import documents, and keep an Obsidian vault in step with Launchway documents in both directions.
items.detail: A plug-in is provided if the sync needs one. Conflicts are shown, not hidden.

groups.name: Move off a self-hosted automation server
groups.blurb: Everything teams rely on such a server for, without its weaknesses.

items.title: A verified gap analysis
items.value: A tested list of what teams rely on automation servers for (dynamic pipelines, extensions, agents anywhere) with a plan for each gap.
items.detail: Each gap names the Launchway feature that closes it and a test that proves it.

items.title: Import of existing jobs
items.value: Convert job definitions and shared libraries, with a report of what needs a person, and none of the file-first configuration or fragile plug-ins.
items.detail: The import produces ordinary pipelines in Git and tells you what it could not convert.

items.title: Extensions without fragility
items.value: A step catalogue and typed custom steps instead of plug-ins that run inside the server.
items.detail: Nothing a team adds can crash or compromise the server, and every extension has a version and an owner.
items.needs: Custom steps in your own language.

items.title: Agents anywhere
items.value: Guidance and checks that show runners on any machine, in any network, replace the build agents teams rely on. Runners that connect outward, with pools and labels, already work.
items.detail: Equivalent to the build agents teams rely on, with identity and audit on every connection.

milestones.name: Delivery and GitOps depth
milestones.promise: See and control everything you run, whether it is an application in a cluster, a virtual machine or an image-based host, and deliver to it safely.
milestones.audience: Teams that deploy to Kubernetes, virtual machines, machine images and clouds, and people who answer for what is running and whether it is healthy.
milestones.what: Milestone 3 is about everything after the build. See every application and host in one place, find out why a deployment failed, roll out safely with weights and checks, run infrastructure as code with state kept for you, manage image-based hosts, and watch traffic, protection and reliability in the same views.
scenarios: A deployment fails. Launchway says in one sentence why, shows the evidence, and offers to roll back the setting that caused it.
You send ten percent of mobile traffic to a new version and watch errors on a map before widening it.
You turn off a misbehaving feature with one button on a page that also shows its effect.
A fleet of image-based hosts upgrades in batches with a check between each, and one batch pauses.
A reviewer sees an automatically written change record with its risk and freeze status.
milestones.diagram:
flowchart TD Image["Image or chart"] --> Plan["Delivery plan
policy, approval"] Plan --> Targets subgraph Targets["Where it runs"] K8s["Kubernetes
Argo CD or built-in"] VMs["Virtual machines"] Hosts["Image-based hosts"] Cloud["Clouds and serverless"] end Targets --> Watch["Watch
health, traffic, errors"] Config["Configuration, secrets, toggles
per zone"] --> Targets Watch -->|verdict| Plan Watch --> Insight["Metrics, changes, incidents"]
milestones.diagramNote: One plan, many targets, and a watch loop that can send a change back.
done: An application, a virtual machine and an image-based host can each be deployed, verified and rolled back from the interface.
A failed deployment shows a diagnosis, its evidence and the full resource tree with logs.
Canary weights by client type work on the gateway and on a mesh, and the map shows them.
State for infrastructure code is stored, locked and recoverable inside Launchway.
Toggles, settings and secrets resolve per zone with one clear rule.
Every lever change goes through preview, policy and audit, with an undo.
notIncluded: The software graph and patching loop (Milestone 5).

groups.name: Applications and rollouts
groups.blurb: See and control everything you run, then deliver to it safely.

items.title: Argo CD in depth
items.value: Application hierarchy views (app-of-apps and ApplicationSet trees) with status, sync, health, history and actions, ready health checks, and a hosted or your own Argo CD.
items.detail: Launchway reads each application as the deploy engine sees it, shows drift, and lets you act with the same permissions as everything else. Argo CD is first-class, never required.

items.title: Applications and ApplicationSets from the interface
items.value: Generate applications and sets, and compose app-of-apps, from a guided screen.
items.detail: The generated manifests are shown as a change you review and merge, so GitOps remains the record.

items.title: Health checks set up from the interface
items.value: Write and test custom health checks for resources without editing configuration by hand.
items.detail: A check shows its result against live resources before you save it.

items.title: Hosted or your own Argo CD
items.value: Use an Argo CD that Launchway runs for you, or connect one you already have.
items.detail: Both are equal in the interface. Teams that do not use Argo CD can use built-in deploys instead.

items.title: Rollout control inside a run
items.value: A pipeline watches a rollout, pauses at gates, promotes or aborts, and shows each step of the rollout as a station.
items.detail: Verification tests run between steps, and the run keeps the evidence.

items.title: A single pane of glass
items.value: One fleet view of every application and every host: what runs where, its health, drift and evidence.
items.detail: Error rates, version, last change and owner are on one screen, and each tile opens the page that explains it.

items.title: Weighted canaries and traffic control
items.value: Send a share of traffic, by client type, to a new version through the Gateway API or a service mesh, with mesh metrics as ready-made health checks.
items.detail: The overlay on the traffic map shows what share each version takes right now.

items.title: Releases across services
items.value: Ship several services as one ordered, gated release with a promotion view across environments.
items.detail: Promotion moves the same digest, never a rebuild, and every step shows who approved it.

items.title: Promotion across environments
items.value: Move a version from one environment to the next with checks and approvals in between.
items.detail: The matrix shows what runs where, which places are behind, and a button to move a version.

items.title: Post-deploy watch and incidents
items.value: Keep watching after release, roll back automatically, and tie incidents to the change that caused them.
items.detail: An incident links back to the commit, run and setting change nearest to it.

items.title: AI analysis as an optional rollback gate
items.value: Let a verification step use AI analysis of metrics and logs to trigger automatic rollback, off by default and able to require a person for production.
items.detail: Plain threshold checks remain the default, and AI can decide only where you allow it.

groups.name: Debug a deployment, then see everything
groups.blurb: Why did it fail, in one sentence, then every resource behind it.

items.title: Why did it fail to deploy
items.value: A failed application opens with a diagnosis in one sentence, the evidence behind it and one recommended action.
items.detail: Each piece of evidence is a button that opens the resource where it shows: manifest, events or log. AI can help word the diagnosis, but the evidence is always facts.

items.title: A timeline of changes and symptoms
items.value: Changes, new copies starting, alerts and health on a single time line, with what changed since it last worked.
items.detail: A comparison with the last working version covers image, settings and manifests.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

items.title: Everything deployed
items.value: The whole resource tree: workloads, pods, containers, services, routes, settings, volumes, jobs and custom resources.
items.detail: Each node has overview, events, manifest with desired against live, and logs. Secrets show by name only.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

items.title: Logs where you need them
items.value: Container logs now and from before the last restart, with search, follow, a time range and jump to the first error.
items.detail: Restarts, exit codes and resource use sit beside the log.

items.title: Fix actions with their consequence
items.value: Roll a setting back, retry an update or open the failing pod, each saying in words what will happen.
items.detail: Every action is a guided change that can be undone and is audited.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

groups.name: Where it deploys
groups.blurb: Clusters, virtual machines, machine images, clouds and serverless.

items.title: Built-in Helm and Kubernetes deploys
items.value: Deploy and roll back without Argo CD; Argo stays first class for long-lived environments.
items.detail: The deploy is a typed step with a plan, a diff, health checks and a rollback to the last good release.

items.title: Preview environments
items.value: Every pull request or branch gets its own environment and address, tested and cleaned up on merge.
items.detail: The pull request page shows the address and the verification result.

items.title: VM deploys
items.value: Roll a change across virtual machines in batches over SSH, with verification between batches.
items.detail: Hosts appear next to applications on the fleet page, with what runs on each.

items.title: Machine images with Packer
items.value: Bake machine images in a pipeline and roll them through instance groups.
items.detail: Images have contents, scan results and signatures like container images.

items.title: Image-based hosts
items.value: Machines that are really images (built on bootc), built, signed, upgraded and rolled back like container images, with host setup done at first boot.
items.detail: Staged upgrades, reboots in batches and a go-back button use the same runway as an application rollout.

items.title: First boot owned by Launchway
items.value: The first-boot unit applies host name, network, keys and zone, and may run a configuration playbook once before the host takes traffic.
items.detail: Running a playbook on a host that is already serving traffic stays refused, because that is what brings drift back.

items.title: Configuration at build time
items.value: Ansible and image builders work together at build time to prepare images.
items.detail: What belongs in the image is baked, and what must differ per host is applied at first boot.

items.title: An infrastructure stack designer
items.value: Compose image, build and configuration blocks visually and have them turned into pipelines.
items.detail: The picture and the generated files stay in step, and the result is reviewable in Git.

items.title: Image as a service for enterprise Linux teams
items.value: Watch base images and advisories, rebuild, re-sign, re-scan and roll out across zones with verification.
items.detail: You can ask whether every production host runs an approved, signed and scanned image patched inside its deadline, and get a yes or a list.

items.title: Hosts and machine images in the interface
items.value: A catalogue of images with contents and base, and a hosts page showing version, staged upgrade, drift and last seen.
items.detail: A host page draws first boot as a short line, with boot history and logs.

items.title: Cloud targets: AWS, Google Cloud and Azure
items.value: Deploy to the three major clouds with their own features, with no stored cloud keys.
items.detail: Each target uses short-lived identity from the pipeline step.

items.title: Serverless and managed instance groups
items.value: Functions, container services and managed instance groups as deploy targets.
items.detail: Rollouts, health checks and rollbacks follow the same model as on Kubernetes.
items.needs: Cloud targets: AWS, Google Cloud and Azure.

groups.name: Infrastructure as code
groups.blurb: State, plans and checks you can trust.

items.title: Terraform and OpenTofu
items.value: Reviewed plans, applies that run only the reviewed plan, state kept and locked inside Launchway, and drift detection.
items.detail: Users never wonder where state goes, and Launchway guides them to good practice by default.

items.title: State and locking built in
items.value: State is stored, versioned and locked inside Launchway with access rules.
items.detail: Nothing external is needed, and the state remains exportable.

items.title: Ansible
items.value: Typed steps with per-host results and a check mode before apply.
items.detail: Results show per host, with the check result shown before anything is changed.

items.title: Chef
items.value: A real step with per-node results where Chef reports them, check mode before apply, and templates.
items.detail: It has the same standing as Ansible, using the free build by default.

items.title: Database change steps
items.value: Apply database schema changes as a pipeline step, with a plan and a rollback where the tool supports it.
items.detail: Changes pass the same gates as other deploys.

items.title: Packer builds as a first-class step
items.value: Run image builds with their results, logs and artifacts attached to the run.
items.detail: Output images go to the registry or the image store with provenance.

groups.name: Runtime configuration
groups.blurb: Settings, keys and toggles managed together, per zone and environment.

items.title: Feature toggles
items.value: A built-in toggle service that applications and agents read, per environment, with percentage and client-type rollouts.
items.detail: It speaks an open protocol, so existing applications can read it with no Launchway library.

items.title: Configuration, keys and toggles per zone
items.value: Manage settings and secrets together per zone and environment, for virtual machines and Kubernetes alike.
items.detail: A zone is a named place and failure domain such as a region or a cluster. The nearest owner wins unless a higher level has enforced the value.

items.title: Routing by client attributes
items.value: Decide which version a request gets from who sent it, such as a share of mobile clients, inside the application or at the network.
items.detail: The effective exposure of route share times toggle share is always shown.

items.title: A guided change for every lever
items.value: Preview, policy check, approval where required, applied and audited, with an undo, for toggles, weights and limits.
items.detail: Moving a lever to its safe state is never gated, and moving away from it always is.

items.title: Secrets with an external store
items.value: Read secrets from more external stores, such as the cloud providers’ own secret services. Vault, OpenBao, files and the environment already work.
items.detail: The store stays authoritative and values never reach the control plane.

items.title: Service mesh support including VMs
items.value: Traffic, identity and policy for services on a mesh, and for virtual machines that join it.
items.detail: Machines outside the mesh still appear on the map as declared.

groups.name: Watch and protect
groups.blurb: See traffic, protect it, and know whether each service is meeting its target.

items.title: A live traffic map
items.value: See how traffic flows between services, workloads and virtual machines, with rates, errors and latency.
items.detail: Each connection says whether it was observed, declared or not observed, and no number is ever made up for one that is not observed.

items.title: Diagnose along a flow
items.value: From a red connection, a one-sentence diagnosis, the failing requests, the pod, the change that caused it and the logs.
items.detail: You go from symptom to cause without changing tools.

items.title: Replay the last hours
items.value: A time slider that replays the last twelve hours of the map with incidents and rollouts marked.
items.detail: Useful for what changed when errors began.

items.title: Inject delays and errors safely
items.value: Add a delay or an error to a share of requests on a healthy connection, with a hard limit on share and time.
items.detail: The dialog shows who is affected, and conditions stop the test early.

items.title: Rate limiting and traffic protection
items.value: Limits per client, route and tenant, connection limits, timeouts, retries and circuit breakers, shown with how close traffic is to each.
items.detail: Changing one is a guided change with a preview that replays the last hour against the new value.

items.title: Attack and abuse signals
items.value: Signs of attack or abuse as plain sentences with evidence and three actions: limit, block or ignore with a reason.
items.detail: Each signal says honestly where it came from.

items.title: Reliability pages
items.value: Services ranked by error budget, saturation and restarts, with deploys, settings, toggles and scaling marked on the charts.
items.detail: Cause and effect are visible on one time line.

items.title: Toggles in context
items.value: Which features are on where and for whom, with the effect of a toggle shown and one button to turn it off.
items.detail: Toggle first, roll back second, in seconds.

items.title: Signal sources
items.value: Connect metrics, logs, analytics, traces, the mesh, a firewall and the toggle service, with a test for each.
items.detail: Every chart names its source and links to the query.

items.title: Service reliability targets
items.value: Set targets for the services you run and see whether a release is spending the budget.
items.detail: Targets can be imported and exported in an open format.

groups.name: Change and insight
groups.blurb: Know what changed, who approved it, and how delivery is going.

items.title: Change management
items.value: Automatic change records with risk scores, freezes and approvals, and optional two-way sync with an IT service tool.
items.detail: Works standalone, so a team without such a tool still has records.

items.title: Connections to ServiceNow and Jira Service Management
items.value: Create and update change records in ServiceNow or Jira Service Management and take their approval back.
items.detail: Optional and equal to the built-in records.

items.title: Delivery metrics and executive dashboards
items.value: Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore, with drill-down to the runs behind each number.
items.detail: Graphs are meant for people who do not use Launchway daily.

items.title: Test intelligence and flow insights
items.value: Find slow and flaky tests, bottlenecks in review and idle time in delivery.
items.detail: Suggestions are shown with the evidence.

items.title: Policy rules in an open language
items.value: Write extra policy rules in an open policy language alongside the built-in rules.
items.detail: Rules run at the same decision point and are shown in the verdict.

items.title: Portfolio bill of materials
items.value: A bill of materials across every image as well as every project, with export. Searching components across projects already works.
items.detail: Pairs with the software graph.

items.title: Experiments with toggles
items.value: Compare outcomes between users with a toggle on and off.
items.detail: Results join delivery data, so you see effect and cost.

groups.name: Moving over from other delivery platforms
groups.blurb: Importers and proof for teams that already have a delivery platform.

items.title: Importers for other delivery platforms
items.value: Convert pipelines, services and environments from other delivery and GitOps platforms, with a report of what needs a person.
items.detail: The report is honest about gaps.

items.title: Published proof points
items.value: Measured comparisons of footprint, speed and capabilities that anyone can reproduce.
items.detail: Methods and results are published.

items.title: Enterprise readiness checklist
items.value: Answers to the questions an enterprise reviewer asks, with a support bundle and an evidence page.
items.detail: Close the gaps that gate adoption.

milestones.name: A built-in registry
milestones.promise: Images, Helm charts and other OCI artifacts stored beside the code, under the same permissions and policies.
milestones.audience: Teams that want images and charts stored beside the code, with the same permissions, policy and audit and nothing else to run.
milestones.what: Milestone 4 adds a registry to the binary. Images, charts and other artifacts are stored in the same database and blob store as everything else, promoted by digest, cleaned up without ever deleting what is deployed, and checked by policy on the way in and on the way out. Any other registry stays equally supported.
scenarios: A build pushes an image; policy refuses it because it is unsigned.
You promote the exact image tested in staging to production with no copy.
Retention cleans old images but keeps the one a cluster is running.
A project's packages tab shows its images and charts and where each runs.
milestones.diagram:
flowchart TD Build["Build"] -->|push| Gate["Policy on push"] Gate --> Store["Registry
database + blob store"] Store --> Scan["Scan, sign, record"] Scan --> Promote["Promote by digest"] Promote --> Deploy["Policy on deploy"] Deploy --> Run["Running"] Public["Public registries"] -->|pull-through cache| Store Store -->|replicate| Other["Other registries"] Retention["Retention"] -.->|never deletes deployed| Store
milestones.diagramNote: An image from build to running, with policy at both ends.
done: The OCI conformance suite passes.
Docker, container runtimes and Helm work against it with no special setup.
Retention never deletes an image that is deployed, proven by a test.
Promotion by digest moves no bytes.
A registry operation is available in the API, the command line, the agent endpoint and Terraform.
notIncluded: Package formats beyond the first set, which come in order of demand.

groups.name: The registry
groups.blurb: Images, charts and other artifacts stored beside the code, under the same permissions.

items.title: A built-in OCI registry
items.value: Store container images, Helm charts and other OCI artifacts in Launchway, passing the OCI conformance suite, with nothing else to run.
items.detail: It lives in the same database and blob store as everything else, so permissions, audit, quotas and retention are one model. The protocol is small and well specified, so the hard parts are cleanup, tenancy and policy.

items.title: Helm charts and other artifacts as first-class
items.value: Charts, signatures, bills of materials, attestations, operating-system images and WebAssembly modules are stored and shown properly.
items.detail: A chart page shows its versions, which applications use which, and the values it accepts.

items.title: An image page that tells the whole story
items.value: Where an image runs now, tags, layers, vulnerabilities with fixes, contents, signature, provenance and the run and commit that built it.
items.detail: Its history is drawn as a line: built, scanned, signed, in test, in production.

items.title: Promotion by digest
items.value: Move an image from one environment to the next without copying or rebuilding it.
items.detail: What was tested is exactly what ships.

items.title: Retention that protects what runs
items.value: Clean up old images without ever deleting one that is deployed.
items.detail: The label says why each item is kept, such as kept because deployed.

items.title: Policy on push and deploy
items.value: The same policy engine checks an image when it is pushed to the built-in registry, as it already does for a push from a pipeline and for a deploy.
items.detail: Unsigned, unscanned or vulnerable images can be refused at either point.

items.title: Pull-through cache
items.value: Cache public images so builds are faster and unaffected by rate limits.
items.detail: Cached images are scanned and counted against quotas like any other.

items.title: Image guard for sandboxed builds
items.value: Keep unchecked images away from sandboxed builds, and fetch every image through a checking proxy.
items.detail: Names that resolve to private addresses are refused.

items.title: Replication with other registries
items.value: Copy images to and from other registries on a rule.
items.detail: Useful for a disaster-recovery copy or a customer-facing mirror.

items.title: Per-project packages and permissions
items.value: A packages tab in each project that is a filtered view of the registry, with per-package access.
items.detail: The registry and the code share one permission model.

items.title: Signing and verification
items.value: Sign images on build and verify signatures on pull and deploy.
items.detail: Signatures and attestations are stored next to the image.

items.title: More package formats
items.value: Language and system packages, such as for common programming languages, with cleanup rules and quotas.
items.detail: Added in order of demand, with a shared storage model.

items.title: Any other registry, equally
items.value: Pushing to any OCI registry works today and stays first class beside the built-in one.
items.detail: Choose per project and move later.

milestones.name: The software graph, with automated patching
milestones.promise: One connected picture of code, dependencies, images and deployments, so you always know what runs where and can fix it safely.
milestones.audience: Teams and security groups who need to know what runs where, what it is made of and how to fix it safely.
milestones.what: Milestone 5 connects code, dependencies, images and deployments in one graph kept in Launchway's own database. It answers what is running, from what, containing what and is any of it vulnerable. Patching then becomes an ordinary change that goes through tests, change management and a controlled rollout.
scenarios: A new advisory arrives; Launchway lists the services affected and who owns each.
You search for a function across every repository you can see.
Automatic patching is switched on for one zone; a dependency update arrives as a change, passes its tests and rolls out.
An agent asks which services use a library and gets an answer from the graph, not from reading files.
milestones.diagram:
flowchart TD Code["Code and commits"] --> Graph[("Software graph")] Deps["Packages and licences"] --> Graph Img["Images and charts"] --> Graph Dep["Deployments and hosts"] --> Graph Adv["Advisories"] --> Graph Graph --> Q["Questions
what, where, who, how bad"] Graph --> Patch["Patch proposal"] Patch --> Review["Tests and change management"] Review --> Roll["Rollout and verification"] Roll --> Dep
milestones.diagramNote: The graph is built from facts Launchway already records, keyed by what is deployed.
done: For any running image Launchway can show its commit, run, components and findings.
A new advisory re-scores running software without a rebuild.
An automated patch reaches production only through the same gates as any change.
Patching can be switched off per zone and is off by default.
notIncluded: Cost management and the developer portal (Beyond).

groups.name: Know what you run
groups.blurb: One connected picture of code, dependencies, images and deployments.

items.title: Findings and SBOMs per run
items.value: The starting point already works: findings and components recorded for every run.
items.detail: Components are recorded as bills of materials and findings are kept with the run.

items.title: What is deployed where
items.value: Link every deployed image back to its commit, its components and its findings, including on hosts Launchway only observes.
items.detail: Facts are keyed by image digest and by deployment, so one query can answer across Git, the registry, scans and the deploy engine.

items.title: A continuous observer of what runs
items.value: Watch clusters and hosts for what is actually running, not only what was deployed.
items.detail: Surprises, such as an image nobody deployed, are flagged.

items.title: Continuous scanning of what runs
items.value: Scan deployed software for new vulnerabilities and best-practice gaps, not only at build time.
items.detail: A new advisory re-scores everything already running.

items.title: Advisories, exceptions and licences
items.value: Record which vulnerabilities apply, import vendor statements that they do not, and check licences.
items.detail: A finding can be waived with a reason and an expiry.

items.title: Who owns what
items.value: Each component, service and repository has an owner, and findings go to that owner.
items.detail: Questions like which services use this library get an answer.

items.title: Code search across repositories
items.value: Search symbols and text across every repository, hosted or connected, filtered by what you may see.
items.detail: Results include pipelines, templates and steps.

items.title: Code intelligence
items.value: Definitions, references and call information, for people and for agents.
items.detail: Gives agents the context they need without sending whole repositories.

items.title: Code knowledge for AI, with fewer tokens
items.value: Answer AI questions from a graph of code and deployments instead of pasting files.
items.detail: Fewer tokens are sent and the answers cite where they came from.

items.title: Blast radius of a vulnerability
items.value: From an advisory, see which deployed services and environments are affected and who owns them.
items.detail: The list becomes a set of proposed fixes.

groups.name: Fix it safely
groups.blurb: Patch as a normal change, with checks and a controlled rollout.

items.title: Automated patching
items.value: Off by default and turned on per zone: updates open as changes, pass tests and change management, and roll out through Argo CD.
items.detail: The loop is propose, test, approve, roll out and verify, and every step is recorded.

items.title: Built-in dependency updates
items.value: Keep common ecosystems' dependencies current, as ordinary reviewable pull requests.
items.detail: Updates carry their release notes and test results.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: Image refresh and patching of base images
items.value: Rebuild images when their base changes and roll the new ones out.
items.detail: Fits into the same patching loop and its deadlines.

items.title: AI-proposed fixes
items.value: An optional helper proposes a fix or an upgrade note, flagged as AI, never merged on its own.
items.detail: A person approves, and everything it did is recorded.

items.title: Patch deadlines and evidence
items.value: Track how long each vulnerability has been open and produce evidence of patching within your own deadline.
items.detail: The question is every production host patched in time answered with a query.

milestones.name: AI as an optional first-class helper
milestones.promise: AI wherever it saves effort, always optional, always off until an administrator turns a purpose on, and never able to hide a failure.
milestones.audience: Anyone who wants AI help with delivery, and anyone who wants it kept out.
milestones.what: Milestone 6 puts AI wherever it saves effort and keeps it entirely optional. A built-in gateway routes to any model with spending limits, local models are first-class, regulated projects have a protected path, and a failing check can never be hidden by a model.
scenarios: An administrator turns on AI explanations for failures only, and sets a monthly limit.
A regulated project is allowed to use only models with recorded data terms.
A step calls the gateway by model name; moving to another provider needs no pipeline change.
You sketch a delivery and are shown a pipeline you can read and edit.
milestones.diagram:
flowchart TD Use["Steps, agents, interface"] --> Gate["Purpose switch
off until enabled"] Gate --> Comp["Context compression"] Comp --> GW["Model gateway
limits, usage, routing"] GW --> Local["Local models"] GW --> Cloud["Hosted models"] GW --> Safe["Protected path
recorded data terms"] GW --> Rec["Usage and audit record"]
milestones.diagramNote: Every AI call passes the purpose switch, and every call is recorded.
done: With every AI purpose off, no model is ever called.
Spending limits stop or warn before a budget is exceeded.
Compression never removes file paths, line numbers or error codes, and marks each omission.
A regulated project cannot reach a model it is not allowed to use.
A model verdict never overrides a failing check.
notIncluded: Anything that decides without an explicit setting.

groups.name: Today
groups.blurb: What already works.

items.title: Models in steps and verification
items.value: Hosted or local models in steps, with explanations of failures and verdicts that never override a failing check.
items.detail: Models are configured once and used by name.

items.title: Agents as users
items.value: The agent endpoint gives agents the same permissions, limits and audit as any user.
items.detail: An agent connects with a token and the same rules as a person.

groups.name: A gateway of your own
groups.blurb: One endpoint for every model, with limits and monitoring.

items.title: A built-in model gateway
items.value: One endpoint that routes to any hosted or self-hosted model, with usage monitoring and easy switching of providers.
items.detail: Applications and steps call one address and a model name. Outside gateways remain an optional integration.

items.title: Local and self-hosted models
items.value: Run and serve open models on your own machines and use them like any other.
items.detail: Useful where data cannot leave the building.

items.title: Provider switching and fallbacks
items.value: Change provider or model in one place, with fallbacks if one is down.
items.detail: No code changes in pipelines.

items.title: Usage monitoring
items.value: See usage by model, project and purpose, with cost.
items.detail: Charts feed the same dashboards as everything else.

items.title: Spending limits
items.value: Budgets in money, per model, project and purpose, not only in tokens.
items.detail: Calls stop or warn when a limit is reached.

items.title: AI off until a purpose is turned on
items.value: Every purpose, such as explaining failures or reviewing changes, is off until an administrator turns it on.
items.detail: Nothing is sent to a model by surprise.

items.title: Context compression
items.value: Shrink what is sent to a model without losing file paths, line numbers or error codes, with every omission marked and the saving measured.
items.detail: Never breaks a provider's prompt cache, and the saving is shown in money.

items.title: A protected path for regulated data
items.value: Use only models whose data-handling terms you have recorded, so that regulated projects never reach the wrong one.
items.detail: Adapters for the big cloud model services are included.

items.title: Models that know Launchway
items.value: Optional models tuned on Launchway itself, runnable locally and never trained on customer data.
items.detail: They answer questions about the product and write configuration.

items.title: From a picture to a pipeline
items.value: Design a delivery visually and have AI help translate it into a pipeline you can read and edit.
items.detail: Output is a proposed change in Git, never applied unseen.

items.title: AI summaries and review of changes
items.value: Optional summaries and review comments on pull requests, labelled as AI.
items.detail: It never approves or merges.
items.needs: Pull requests on the built-in host.

items.title: AI help with failures
items.value: Explain why a deploy failed as well as a step, with the evidence used. Explaining a failed step already works.
items.detail: Always shows the facts first.
items.needs: Why did it fail to deploy.

items.title: Agent guidance and an agent catalogue
items.value: Ready-made instructions so agents know how to use Launchway, and a list of agents with their permissions.
items.detail: Each agent is audited like a user.

milestones.name: The hosted service, the public demo and enterprise controls
milestones.promise: Use Launchway without running it, on a plan that follows your choices, with the controls enterprises and regulated teams ask for.
milestones.audience: Teams that want Launchway as a service, evaluators who want to try it, and enterprises and regulated teams that need strong identity, audit and compliance.
milestones.what: Milestone 7 lets you use Launchway without running it. Organisations are isolated, runners on your machines connect out, hosted steps run in isolated machines, and a public demo is available. The same milestone adds the identity, audit and retention controls enterprises ask for.
scenarios: You sign up, connect a runner on your own cluster and run a pipeline without any of your code leaving your network.
A regulated team enables encryption keys with rotation and a retention rule.
An auditor exports a tamper-evident audit trail to the security tools.
A visitor explores the public demo with realistic data.
